USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Continue negotiating from the current position of strength without escalating and without conceding leverage. Keep the $250bn tariff overhang (especially the suspended threat to raise List 3 from 10% to 25%) as the central bargaining chip, and hold out for a verifiable enforcement mechanism on structural IP/forced-tech-transfer issues before agreeing to any tariff rollback. Do not break the truce by escalating now, and do not surrender tariffs before China delivers verified commitments.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to US interests is modest and tilted toward opportunity, not danger. The US holds the initiative: China has recommitted to increased purchases (US exports to China rose ~49% to $10.6bn in the latest month) and has kept the yuan strong at ~6.71 rather than devaluing it as a countermeasure (country_health DRXCHUS/DEXCHUS). The dispute is on a de-escalating track - the March 1 tariff hike was suspended (event timeline 2019-02-24, 2019-03-01) - and markets are calm (VIX ~13, consumer sentiment back to 98.4). That favors the USA's leverage anchor rather than an existential one. However, it is not a clear-cut opportunity either: industrial production is drifting lower (~-1% over the window), the 10-year at 2.61% has the yield curve flirting with inversion - a growth/recession signal the trade war partially feeds - and the farm belt remains exposed to Chinese retaliation, while no final deal exists and Lighthizer himself (NYT, 2019-03-12) concedes the enforcement mechanism and structural reforms are unresolved and could still collapse into re-escalation. On the action axis, the situation justifies holding/negotiating rather than escalating or conceding. Escalation to 25% now would break the truce at the exact moment the US economy is decelerating and the curve is flattening, and would hit US consumers and farmers; conceding tariff rollback before an enforceable, verifiable deal would squander the leverage China's purchase commitments and yuan strength show the US currently holds. The disciplined play is to keep negotiating from strength - use the tariff overhang to extract an enforcement mechanism and structural IP commitments - and only then consider a phased rollback tied to verified compliance.
key_factors: US holds negotiating leverage: China committed to increased purchases (exports to China +49%) and yuan appreciating (6.71 vs 6.9), not devaluing
Dispute on de-escalating track: G20 truce holds, List 3 25% hike suspended, March 1 deadline passed without escalation
But no final deal: enforcement mechanism and structural IP/tech-transfer reforms unresolved (Lighthizer, 2019-03-12)
Domestic deceleration: IP down ~1%, 10yr at 2.61% with near-inverted yield curve flags growth concern
Resilience: consumer sentiment back to 98.4, VIX calm ~13, credit spreads stable - no recession signal yet
~$250bn US tariffs ($50bn@25%, $200bn@10%) remain the core leverage; farm belt exposed to Chinese retaliation

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Continue the negotiating track and signal a willingness to expand our purchase commitments (we have already agreed to buy soybeans) to lock in a deal that removes the threat of the List 3 tariff hike from 10% to 25%. Do not escalate, but hold firm on core structural red lines (forced technology transfer, industrial subsidies) and keep the Huawei/Meng matter separate from the trade settlement so we do not trade away sovereignty over a national champion.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat is genuinely high but not existential. US tariffs now cover ~$250B of our goods (25% on $50B, 10% on $200B), and the pain is visible in the real economy: February exports plunged ~21% y/y, the worst in three years (CNN), the official manufacturing PMI contracted to 49.4 in December (first contraction in over two years, Reuters), and growth has slowed to its lowest since the 2008 crisis. The Huawei/Meng criminal charges (Jan 28 DOJ indictment) add firm-level targeting of a flagship 5G champion, pushing this toward the upper end. But the threat is capped below existential for three PIT reasons: the US has twice postponed the March 1 List 3 hike (Feb 24), Lighthizer says a deal on forced tech transfer and subsidies is 'very close' (Politico), and a Mar-a-Lago summit between Trump and Xi is being floated for late March. The US has clear incentive to settle ahead of 2020, which is leverage for us. Because escalation would deepen the export hit and a near-term settlement is achievable, the right stance is to hold the negotiating posture rather than confront — forward progress and purchase commitments are the cheapest route to easing the tariff overhang that is actively damaging our exporters.
